stimulus.text:
“The Congress shall have Power To lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises, to pay the Debts and provide for the common Defence and general Welfare of the United States; . . . To borrow Money on the credit of the United States; . . . To regulate Commerce with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes; . . . To coin Money, regulate the Value thereof, and of foreign Coin, and fix the Standard of Weights and Measures; . . . To establish Post Offices and post Roads; . . . To declare War, grant Letters of Marque and Reprisal, and make Rules concerning Captures on Land and Water; . . . To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers, and all other Powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any Department or Officer thereof.”

—Constitution of the United States, Article I, Section 8, September 17, 1787

books.section: Topic 3.9 The Constitution, A. The Structure of Government Under the Constitution

primary_sources: Constitution of the United States, Article I, Section 8 (September 17, 1787)

stem: Which of the following best explains why the framers listed Congress’s powers in Section 8 instead of giving Congress a general power to make any law it wished?

options.text: They wanted Congress to share its lawmaking power equally with the president.
options.misconception: Lawmaking belongs to Congress under Article I, Section 1; the president does not share it.

options.text: They expected the states to list their own powers in the same section.
options.misconception: Section 8 lists only the national government’s powers; the states’ powers are covered elsewhere.

options.text: They wanted Congress limited to the powers listed, plus what carries them out.
They believed Congress would never need any power beyond those listed.
options.misconception: The necessary and proper clause shows they expected new needs to arise.

rationales.C: Background: a list of powers, called enumerated powers, limits Congress to what is named, and the elastic clause covers only what carries those powers out.
rationales.A: Background: Article I, Section 1 vests all legislative power in Congress, not in the president.
rationales.B: Section 8 names the national government’s powers; it says nothing about the states’ powers.
rationales.D: The elastic clause at the end of the list shows the framers expected new needs.
rationales.general:
1. Section 8 names Congress’s powers one by one instead of granting a general lawmaking power.
2. A list works as a limit: what is not listed is not granted.
3. The elastic clause only reaches laws that carry the listed powers into effect.
4. So the list itself is the framers’ way of keeping Congress bounded.
Remember: in the Constitution, a list of powers is also a limit on power.
